title: Ops vs growth standoff
theme: Sana and Aditya want opposite things. Run the meeting and land a decision.
practised: Understanding each stakeholder's position before a meeting
Running a decision meeting with people who disagree
Using data to settle an argument
Writing a decision note with trade-offs
story_so_far: Day 1: weak repeat comes from failed first orders (31% vs 6% repeat) and coupon customers (8% vs 25%). Day 2: three customer groups; focus first on morning commuters, who need reliable speed. Day 3: Café loses about ₹82 lakh a month; reaching 30% repeat would make it about +₹30 lakh a month; extra morning staff cost about ₹14 lakh a month; a Pune 3 km radius cap would save about ₹17 lakh a month. Anita wants a go or no-go at the leadership review.
world_today: Today is Thursday of week 1. Three proposals are on the table for fixing first orders, and Sana and Aditya disagree on all three. Meera has called a decisions meeting and wants the player to run it.
canon_after_day: Meera approved a two-week pilot: (1) cap Pune delivery at 3 km; (2) a 'Fast Lane' morning menu (12 items, 7–11 am) in all 18 Pune kitchens and the 20 busiest Bengaluru kitchens; (3) coupons only on a customer's first order; (4) extra morning staff in those kitchens. Aditya gets a targeted 'sorry' credit for customers whose first order goes wrong. Together these become the 'First Order Promise'. The radius cap will be reviewed after two weeks; Aditya has agreed, but is worried about Pune's growth target.

inbox.subject: You're running today's decisions meeting
inbox.body:
Three proposals, two strong opinions. Sana wants them; Aditya hates them:

1. Cap Pune delivery at 3 km from a kitchen.
2. A 'Fast Lane' morning menu: cut 7–11 am items from 34 to 12 to speed up prep.
3. Coupons only on a customer's first order.

Talk to Sana and Aditya one-to-one first so nothing surprises you. Then run the meeting in the 'Café decisions meeting' room. I'll be there, but I want you to drive. End of day, send me a decision note.

Meera

group_chats.name: Café decisions meeting
group_chats.opener: Meera: Okay, everyone's here. Over to you to run this.

tasks.title: Pre-meet Sana and Aditya
tasks.description: Understand what each of them cares about and what they'd accept. Bring evidence into the meeting.

tasks.title: Run the decisions meeting
tasks.description: In the 'Café decisions meeting' room, take the group to a clear recommendation on all three proposals.

tasks.title: Handle the twist
tasks.description: Something will come up in the meeting. Deal with it.

tasks.title: Decision note to Meera
tasks.description: The decision on each proposal, the options considered, trade-offs (who loses what), how we'll know it worked, and when we'll revisit.

message.text: Meeting room is open whenever you're ready.
Aditya (in the meeting): Look, I'll be blunt. Rohan wants Pune at 5,000 orders a day by December. A radius cap takes us backwards to 2,000. I can't sign up to that.

ai_reply.direction: Approve or push back in 2–3 lines. Ask one question about how they'll handle Rohan's Pune target.

scoring.strong_player: Learns each side's real concern before the meeting (Sana: cold, late orders; Aditya: Rohan's Pune target); brings data (far orders: 22% complaints, 4% repeat; the cap lifts Pune margin from −₹31 to −₹9; the menu trial cut prep to 4.5 min for −₹6 order value; his past second-order discount repeated at 9%); keeps the meeting on decisions; reframes the Pune target (orders that lose money and never repeat aren't growth); proposes time-boxed pilots with reversal criteria; gives Aditya something real (a targeted credit); writes a decision note with trade-offs and a revisit date.

expected_answers.t1: Ask each what worries them most and what they'd need to agree. Learn Sana's evidence (the 12-item trial) and Aditya's real constraint (Rohan's 5,000 orders a day in Pune). Get Lakshmi's numbers on far orders and the cap's impact before the meeting.
expected_answers.t2: Open with the goal (fix first orders to lift repeat), take the proposals one at a time, use numbers instead of opinions, invite Karthik to confirm the changes are quick, and close with a clear recommendation and owners.
expected_answers.t3: Acknowledge the target, then reframe: orders beyond 3 km have 22% complaints and 4% repeat and lose money, so they don't get us to 5,000 sustainable orders. Propose the cap as a two-week pilot with a review, plus a plan to widen the radius again once delivery is reliable (new kitchens or faster riders). Offer to explain the numbers to Rohan together.
expected_answers.t4: Decision: pilot all three for two weeks in Pune and the 20 busiest Bengaluru kitchens, plus extra morning staff and a targeted sorry credit for failed first orders. Options considered: do nothing, Bengaluru only, full rollout. Trade-offs: Pune orders drop about 35% short term; Aditya loses blanket coupons. Success: first-order on-time rate, complaints, 7-day repeat, margin per order. Revisit in two weeks; Meera decides; Rohan informed.

common_mistakes: Walking into the meeting without knowing Aditya's real constraint
Letting the meeting become an opinion fight
Siding fully with one person and ignoring the other's concern
Treating Rohan's target as either untouchable or irrelevant
A note with no success measures or revisit date
scoring.senior_view: A senior PM would pre-wire both stakeholders, bring three numbers that settle the argument, and turn 'yes or no' into 'pilot for two weeks with clear success measures'. They'd give Aditya a win, take the CEO target head-on with data, and leave with written decisions and owners.
scoring.drill: Pick a disagreement from your own work. Write one paragraph each side would agree is a fair summary of their view, then one sentence proposing a time-boxed test.
